job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Grace Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents and my grandfather in a small house, and I share a room with my cousin Rosa when she stays over. Mornings I help my mother with her catering orders, then I apply for software jobs for three hours. I sometimes use an AI tool to polish my cover letters, and on Wednesdays I go to a parish youth group that I help run.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What was the last stretch of study like, and what are you hoping for next?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I studied computer science and passed with an average mark. My final project was an inventory app for my aunt's bakery, so she can see what's running out. I had no internship, as firms picked people with placements, and about 65 applications have brought four rejections and a lot of silence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds about right. Work stays work, and the way to get on is to be reliable and keep learning. At church I'd say there's no need to be afraid of every new thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, nothing improves for me. Software jobs for graduates with a pass are hard to get, and my debt hasn't gone anywhere. My parents never say anything, but I see them counting the bills and I'm another mouth at the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, aim for 12 a week, and I'd look at smaller local firms who'd like someone who can fix a website or an app. I'd help my mother with catering for pay, and put a bit toward my loan. I'd also ask my aunt to be a reference for the inventory app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired. I'd say patient but tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your family say about the jobs you apply for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father says take anything honest. My mother says wait for the right one. I'd say they're both right, which doesn't help me decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My phone plan and the few evenings out with friends. I'd keep the parish youth group, because it's what keeps me steady.

There's no need to be afraid of every **new thing**.

Ask my aunt to be a **reference** for the inventory app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change but not the end of the world. People adapted when computers arrived and they'll adapt now. At church I'd say we should help those who struggle and not look down on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's exactly my field that gets squeezed. Coding and checking are what AI does best. The jobs I'd apply for, junior developer and tester, are the ones firms will cut first, and I don't have a placement to stand out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get serious about the AI tools instead of using them now and then. I'd take a course in building apps using AI assistants and show my work to small firms. I'd also look at roles like support and onboarding in software firms, where a person is still wanted. I'd put 15 a week aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but ready. I'd say like waiting for exam results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does adapting look like for you, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop doing it the old way. If a tool can write the repeated parts, I'd spend my time on the customer's problem and checking the result. That's what I did for my aunt's bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Rosa, who works in an office doing data entry. My cousin Rosa would be among the first affected and I don't think she's thought about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for ordinary families and the people in charge should be honest about it. I'd say churches and communities need to be ready to help neighbours, because governments will be slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened. If AI does all thinking work better and cheaper, there's nothing left for a junior developer, and I'd be among the first the firms stop hiring. I'd have two months of money, and my parents' catering depends on orders from firms that might shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for a hands-on trade, maybe an electrical or care apprenticeship, since robots come three years later. I'd help my mother grow the catering business. I'd cut spending to nothing extra, pay the minimum on my loan and ask the parish if any members are hiring. I'd stay at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd lie awake with it, and pray.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why care work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's something people trust people with. A robot might do the lifting, but families want a person they know sitting with their mother or father. That feels like a job with a future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your cousin Rosa?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To start looking now, and to learn something with people in it. I'd say it gently, because Rosa doesn't like being told, but better she hears it from me.

Churches and communities need to be ready to help **neighbours**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good warning and we should get on with it. I'd say people should learn how to work with the tools, and the government should keep out of it unless it has to step in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm cautiously hopeful. If I can get a first job in the next year, I'd be building skills while it happens. Experience with AI tools and real customers would help, and I've got the bakery app to show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim for any software role with customer contact, and I'd learn one new tool a month. I'd put 100 a month toward a savings account, and help my mother make the catering business less dependent on one client. I'd keep running the parish group, because mentoring teenagers is a skill that holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful but watchful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for your mother's catering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Set up online ordering and a simple customer list, so my mother isn't relying on two firms. I could build it in a month and she'd have something of her own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no job comes in the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd run the ordering system and any similar small jobs for other family businesses. It's not a career, but it's honest work and it builds a record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and we shouldn't waste it worrying. I'd say people should learn, families should save and communities should stay close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I'd say it's manageable. A decade is enough to get a job, pay my loan and maybe marry. The risk is that I'd feel safe, and the change would come with no warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first decent job, even outside software, and keep upskilling. I'd save 150 a month, help my parents pay down the house and maybe save for a wedding. I'd also keep using AI in small ways and look at a part-time masters when I can afford it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. I'd say settled, which surprises me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the masters be for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might give me a path into a firm that sponsors people. And I'd like to understand how these systems work, not only use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still bother you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That my parents are older. In ten years they'd be retired on a small pension. I'd want to be able to help them, and that means I need steady work, not a good idea.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I'd be the exact person firms stop hiring, and my family couldn't carry me and my loan. What would help is apprenticeships that pay, church and family staying close and honest warnings from people in charge.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I don't want to be a burden. I'd rather be useful to my family and my parish, and a job is the way to do that.

headlineQuote: I don't want to be a burden. I'd rather be useful to my family and my parish, and a job is the way to do that.
portrait: Grace is a 23-year-old **computer science** graduate with a pass, no internship and about 65 applications.
She lives with her parents and grandfather, helps her mother's **catering** and runs a parish youth group.
She is traditional, favours work over handouts and uses AI tools **now and then** for letters.
Her mood is **anxious** for most worlds, alarmed at two years and uneasy but settled when she has a decade.
Her plans lean on **family business**, care or trade work as a hedge, and mentoring in her parish.
biggestWorry: The **2028** case, when firms stop hiring juniors like her and family couldn't carry her loan.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **apprenticeships**, church and family staying close, and honest warnings.
